title: Home Service Booking Rate: Find Where Inquiries Get Lost
searchTitle: Home Service Booking Rate: Find Where Inquiries Get Lost
excerpt: Calculate your home service booking rate, separate missed calls from poor fit and capacity limits, and decide what to fix before buying more leads.
content:
Before buying more leads, check how many suitable inquiries become booked jobs. Count each opportunity once, define what qualifies, and track the result. A thin schedule can come from too few inquiries, poor fit, slow response, or a lack of available appointments. Those need different fixes.

Your booking rate helps you choose the next move. It doesn't diagnose the whole business by itself.

Calculate your home service booking rate with a clear denominator

For this audit, use booked opportunities ÷ eligible inquiries × 100. An eligible inquiry is a genuine request for a service you offer, in an area you serve. Include suitable work you couldn't schedule; capacity is part of what you're checking.

Count one customer's request once, even if they call twice and submit a form. Exclude spam, vendor calls, and duplicate contacts. Record the exclusions so next month's number uses the same rules.

Here's a hypothetical example: 40 inbound contacts include six repeat contacts and four spam or unrelated requests. That leaves 30 eligible inquiries. If 12 become bookings, the rate is 12 ÷ 30 × 100 = 40%.

That does not mean 60% of the ad budget was wasted. Inquiries have different sources, costs, job values, and outcomes. It means 18 suitable opportunities didn't become bookings within the period you measured.

Follow one group of inquiries through to an outcome

Start with inquiries received during one week. Give each one a row in a notebook or spreadsheet:

  • Date received and source, if known.
  • Service requested and whether it qualifies.
  • Time of first human response.
  • Booked, awaiting a decision, declined, unreachable, or no capacity.
  • Reason for the outcome, when the customer actually gives one.

Don't count an unanswered call as a lost job or assume a silent customer rejected your price. Keep unknowns visible. Review the same group again after the normal decision window for that type of work.

A furnace repair request and a planned bathroom remodel shouldn't share an arbitrary seven-day deadline. Split urgent service and planned projects before comparing rates.

Find the constraint before choosing the fix

Suitable inquiries are going unanswered: assign call coverage or a callback owner. Set a response target your team can safely meet, and measure actual response times. A target is an operating choice, not a universal promise about booking lift.

Customers are asking for work you don't do: check the ad, profile, and page that generated the inquiry. Clearer service boundaries may help more than faster callbacks.

Customers want dates you can't offer: review capacity and scheduling. Buying more of the same inquiries may add cost without creating room for the work.

Estimates are waiting on a decision: use a separate estimate follow-up process. Agree on the next contact and make it useful; one unanswered message doesn't explain why a job is still open.

Make the callback useful

When you return a call, identify yourself, confirm the service needed, and explain the next available step. Don't promise same-day service unless you can deliver it.

For a customer who has agreed to text about the request, a starting message could be:

Hi [first name], this is [name] at [company], returning your service inquiry. What do you need help with, and when is a good time to talk?

Use the customer's agreed contact channel. Don't build automatic texts around a phone number alone.

Decide whether more lead spend makes sense

There is no single booking percentage that tells every trade to increase its budget. Look at available capacity, suitable inquiry volume, booked-job cost, and whether the work is profitable.

Change one part of the process, then review another comparable group of inquiries. Record the dates and counts alongside the percentage. A small week's result is a clue to investigate, not proof of a permanent improvement.

Start with your last 30 eligible inquiries. If you can't tell what happened to them, fixing that record is useful work before the next budget decision. The seven-question marketing checkup can help you choose where to look first.

ai_overviews.ai_quick_answer: Calculate booked opportunities divided by eligible inquiries, then multiply by 100. Count each request once and record pending outcomes. Use the result alongside capacity, job value, and reasons for non-booking to choose the next fix.
ai_overviews.ai_faqs:
Q: How do I calculate my home service booking rate?
A: Divide booked opportunities by eligible inquiries and multiply by 100. For example, 12 bookings from 30 eligible inquiries is 40%. Count each request once and use the same eligibility rules each period.

Q: What is a good booking rate?
A: There is no universal target for every trade and job type. Compare consistent groups of inquiries, allowing for job mix, capacity, response time, and the normal decision window.

Q: How often should I follow up on an estimate?
A: Agree on the next contact with the customer. If no date is set, use a short, useful sequence suited to the job and stop when they respond, decline, book, or ask you to stop.
ai_overviews.ai_takeaways:
Define eligible inquiries and count each opportunity once.
Separate urgent service from planned projects and keep open outcomes visible.
Choose the fix from the actual constraint; there is no universal booking-rate threshold.

title: Google Business Profile Optimization: Build a Better Profile
searchTitle: Google Business Profile Optimization: Build a Better Profile
excerpt: Build a useful Google Business Profile with clear steps, sample service descriptions, and a downloadable 30-page website planning map.
content:
You don't need to be a Google expert to build a strong business profile. You need accurate information, a sensible order of work, and clear descriptions of the jobs you do.

If you can explain your work to a customer over the phone, you already have much of what you need. The next step is putting those answers in the right places.

Here's how I'd work through a profile for a local service business. You can use the same steps to improve one you've had for years.

1. Get the business details right

Start with the information someone needs to hire you:

  • Your real business name.
  • A phone number that reaches the business.
  • A working website link.
  • Your customer-facing hours, including holiday changes.
  • An accurate address or service area.

Use your actual business name. Adding “Best Missoula Plumber” to a name that doesn't include those words can violate Google's rules. If you work from home and only travel to customers, follow Google's service-area guidance and hide the residential address. See Google's business guidelines.

If Google is asking you to verify the business, handle that before treating the setup as finished. Also check whether the business already has a profile before creating another one.

2. Choose a category that describes the business

The primary category should describe what your business is. Choose the most specific accurate option Google makes available.

Additional categories should describe other real parts of the business. You don't need a category for every job you might accept. Google explains that distinction in its category guidance.

This is worth doing carefully. A customer looking for a particular trade should be able to recognize that they're in the right place.

3. Write the description from questions customers already ask

Before writing, answer these in plain language:

  • What work do you do?
  • Who do you do it for?
  • Where do you work?
  • What should someone know about working with you?

For a fictional plumbing business, that could become:

We handle drain cleaning, leak repairs, and water heater replacement for homeowners in Missoula. When you contact us, we'll ask what's happening, confirm whether we cover your address, and explain the next step for scheduling a visit.

It tells someone what the company does and what to expect when they call. Compare that with “Your trusted partner for exceptional plumbing solutions,” which could describe almost any plumber and answers very little.

Add details that are true of your business. If you work on older homes, explain the relevant work you handle. If you only take residential jobs, say so. Don't borrow a competitor's promises about availability, experience, or guarantees.

Keep links and promotional offers out of this field. Google's description rules call for useful business information and prohibit links in the description.

4. Give each service its own short explanation

Your main description introduces the company. The service entries let you explain individual jobs.

Where your profile has a services section, list the work you actually offer. A useful way to write each entry is to name the job, describe the problem it addresses, and explain what's included.

Two examples for that fictional plumber:

Drain cleaning: Clearing slow or blocked household drains, including sinks, tubs, and showers. We assess the blockage and explain the recommended work before starting.

Water heater replacement: Removing an existing water heater and installing a replacement. We confirm the equipment and installation scope before providing an estimate.

Use these as examples of structure. Your descriptions should match your own work and process. Google supports service descriptions and, where applicable, prices through its services editor.

5. Give the website the same clear structure

The website linked from your profile should help someone understand the same business. Keep the services, service area, contact details, and availability consistent.

Start with your main services. Give a service its own page when you have enough useful information to explain the job, show relevant work, and answer the customer's questions. Closely related tasks can share a page when that makes more sense.

The map below shows how a fictional plumbing business could organize thirty pages. Use it to choose what you need. A smaller business may only have enough material for a handful of strong pages.

Download the full-size planning map or download the page list as a CSV to make your own plan.

The map in text

01 Home introduces the business and links to its main sections.

Services: 02 Services overview; 03 Drain cleaning; 04 Leak repair; 05 Water heater repair; 06 Water heater replacement; 07 Fixture installation.

Service areas: 08 Service areas overview; 09 Missoula; 10 Lolo; 11 Frenchtown.

Work: 12 Work overview; 13 Drain blockage case study; 14 Leak repair case study; 15 Water heater installation.

Advice: 16 Advice overview; 17 Repair or replace the water heater?; 18 Why drains keep clogging; 19 Find your water shutoff; 20 What happens at a service visit?; 21 How estimates work.

About: 22 About the business; 23 Meet the team; 24 Licenses and insurance; 25 Customer reviews.

Contact: 26 Contact details; 27 Request service; 28 Service FAQs.

Utility pages: 29 Privacy; 30 Accessibility.

These are possible pages, not a list to fill at any cost. Only publish a case study about work you actually did, and only describe credentials you hold. Add a location page when you serve that place and can offer useful local detail. Swapping town names into the same sales copy adds little for the reader and can stray into the practices Google describes as doorway abuse.

There is no Google requirement for thirty pages or a separate website page for every service in your profile. This is a planning example, not a ranking formula.

Share the map with your team. If you reference it on your own website, please credit True Path Digital and link to this guide so readers can find the explanation. An optional image-and-credit snippet is available to copy.

6. Show the work, then explain what we're looking at

Choose real photos that help someone understand your business: a completed installation, a service vehicle, or the entrance customers use to find the shop. Get permission where needed and keep private customer information out of view.

For an update, pair a relevant photo with a short explanation. Here's an example you could adapt after a real job:

Replaced an older water heater in a Missoula home this week. The work included removing the old unit and checking the connections before the replacement went into service.

Only use that wording if it describes the work you did. There is no reason to invent a job story to fill a posting schedule.

Google's post guidance supports updates about the business. Use them when you have something customers need to know, such as a service change, seasonal reminder, or genuine opening in the schedule.

7. Make it easy to leave honest feedback

Use a direct review link so customers don't have to search for the right listing. Apply the same invitation rule regardless of whether you expect a glowing review or a mixed one.

A simple request:

Thank you for choosing us. If you'd like to share your experience, here's our Google review link. Honest feedback is welcome.

Don't offer a reward or ask customers to include service keywords, a staff member's name, or a particular rating. Let them choose what to say. Those limits come from Google's review policy.

8. Try to hire yourself from your phone

Open the public profile and pick a service you offer. Could someone unfamiliar with your company work out whether you handle it, where you work, and how to contact you?

Tap the website link. Find the service information. Check the phone number and what happens when someone calls during your listed hours.

You may find a simple mismatch: the profile advertises weekend availability, but the website says calls are returned Monday. Correct both so the customer knows what to expect.

Once the basics are in place, keep them current when the business changes. A useful monthly reminder is to check the contact details, hours, links, and reviews. That schedule is a suggestion for staying organized, not a Google ranking requirement.

Google describes local ranking through relevance, distance, and prominence. A clearer profile can help customers understand the business, but it doesn't guarantee a particular Maps position. Google's local ranking guidance explains those limits.

Start by rewriting one service description so it answers the questions you hear on the phone. Then check that a customer can reach you from it. If you'd like help reviewing the whole profile, see my Google Business Profile optimization service.

ai_overviews.ai_quick_answer: You can handle the basics without being a Google expert. Start with accurate details, choose suitable categories, and explain the jobs you do. Use real photos and honest review requests, then check that a customer can contact you from the profile.
ai_overviews.ai_faqs:
Q: Do I need to be an expert to improve my Google Business Profile?
A: You can handle the basic business details and write useful service descriptions yourself. Follow the current guidelines and get help if you run into an eligibility, verification, or suspension issue.

Q: How often should I update my profile?
A: Correct the profile when your business details change. Add posts when you have useful news. A monthly check of hours, contact details, links, and reviews is a suggested routine, not a Google ranking requirement.

Q: Will these steps guarantee a better Google Maps ranking?
A: No. Local ranking also depends on distance, competition, relevance, and prominence. These steps help you describe the business accurately and make it easier for customers to understand and contact you.

Q: Does my website need thirty pages to support my profile?
A: No. The map is a planning example. Create only the pages you can make useful and accurate. Google does not require a separate website page for every profile service.
ai_overviews.ai_takeaways:
Write from the questions customers already ask about your work.
Use the description to introduce the business and service entries to explain individual jobs.
Check the phone number, website link, and hours before calling the setup finished.
Use the 30-page website map to choose useful pages, not to fill a quota.

title: Why Marketing Fails Early: Check the Ad-to-Booking Handoff
searchTitle: Why Marketing Fails Early: Check the Ad-to-Booking Handoff
excerpt: Find where marketing breaks: ad delivery, the landing page, inquiry tracking, or follow-through. Use a service-business example to choose one useful fix.
content:
Marketing can stall at several different points: the ad doesn't show, the wrong person clicks, the page doesn't answer their question, or nobody handles the inquiry. Find the broken handoff before changing the whole campaign.

Clear copy matters. So do delivery settings, budget, competition, a working page, and reliable follow-through. Blaming every weak result on the message can send you looking in the wrong place.

First, check whether the campaign can deliver

If an ad barely shows, check approval status, billing, dates, location targeting, budget, and bidding constraints before rewriting the headline. A good offer can't fix an ineligible ad.

Google's Ad Rank documentation explains that placement depends on several factors, including bids, auction context, competition, and ad and landing-page quality. Better creative is one part of that system. It doesn't guarantee more distribution.

Avoid applying one platform's auction explanation to every other channel. Use the delivery diagnostics available in the account you're reviewing.

Then follow the promise from the ad to the page

Take one real ad and open its destination on your phone. Write down the service, location, and next step the ad promises. Then look for those same details on the page.

Here's a hypothetical HVAC example:

Ad: “Furnace repair in Missoula. Call to check today's availability.”

Weak handoff: a general homepage about heating, cooling, installations, and company history, with the phone number buried below several sections.

Clearer handoff: a furnace-repair page that confirms the service area, explains the diagnostic visit, shows the phone number, and tells the customer how availability is confirmed.

The clearer version answers the request the ad attracted. It still can't promise a booking, and it shouldn't advertise immediate service when the schedule is full.

Keep the message-match checklist

Before changing bids or ordering more creative, check:

  • Can someone explain the offer after reading one sentence?
  • Does the page name the service and area shown in the ad?
  • Does it answer the obvious question about scope, availability, or the next step?
  • Is there relevant proof you can substantiate?
  • Can a phone user call or submit the form without hunting?
  • Does someone receive and handle the inquiry?

Test the form with an identifiable test inquiry and confirm it arrives. A successful screen message doesn't prove the office received it. Don't include test entries in your lead totals.

Read the counts before naming the cause

Use the same date range and keep these measures separate:

  • Impressions: the ad was shown.
  • Clicks: someone selected it.
  • Recorded inquiries: calls or forms that reached the business.
  • Suitable inquiries: requests for work you can actually provide.
  • Booked work: an opportunity became a confirmed booking.

If clicks arrive but recorded inquiries don't, inspect the page and contact route. If inquiries arrive but most are unsuitable, inspect targeting and the offer. If suitable inquiries arrive but sit unanswered, inspect the response process.

These patterns suggest where to investigate. Missing tracking can produce the same apparent gap as poor performance. Don't report zero inquiries when nobody has measured them.

Give the experiment one job

Choose the clearest break and write down what you'll change. For example: “Replace the general homepage destination with the relevant repair page, using the same service promise.” Record the dates and keep other major changes limited where practical.

Review enough activity to understand the result. A few clicks can't tell you which headline wins, and a busy or quiet week can reflect weather, seasonality, or staffing as well as marketing.

If the page is the weak point, start with making the website's next step obvious. If suitable inquiries aren't becoming appointments, check your home service booking rate.

Pick one active ad today. Follow it through to a received inquiry and an assigned person. That is a more useful starting point than changing everything in Ads Manager at once.

ai_overviews.ai_quick_answer: Check ad delivery first, then follow the promise through the landing page, received inquiry, and booking handoff. Keep clicks, suitable inquiries, and booked work separate. Missing tracking must stay unknown rather than being reported as zero.
ai_overviews.ai_faqs:
Q: Should I rewrite the ad when it barely shows?
A: Check eligibility, billing, campaign dates, locations, budget, and bidding constraints first. Creative changes cannot fix every delivery problem.

Q: What does message match mean for a service business?
A: The landing page continues the service, location, and next-step promise made in the ad. It should also explain relevant scope and availability accurately.

Q: Do zero recorded conversions prove the campaign failed?
A: No. Confirm that tracking and inquiry delivery work. Missing measurement can look like poor performance, and a small sample may not support a conclusion.
ai_overviews.ai_takeaways:
An ad can fail to deliver for reasons a headline cannot fix.
Match the service, location, and next step from ad to page.
Confirm inquiries arrive and someone owns the response before judging bookings.

title: How to Follow Up on an Estimate (Before It Goes Cold)
searchTitle: How to Follow Up on an Estimate (Before It Goes Cold)
excerpt: Follow up on an estimate with a clear next step, useful message examples, a respectful stopping point, and a way to measure outcomes without guessing.
content:
The estimate isn't the end of the sale. It's the point where the customer decides whether the scope, price, timing, and working relationship make sense.

Useful follow-up helps them make that decision. Confirm they received the quote, agree on the next contact, and make it easy to ask a question or decline. Silence alone doesn't tell you whether the issue is price, timing, another bidder, or something you left unclear.

Set the next step when you send the estimate

Include a short scope summary, meaningful exclusions, and how to accept or ask questions. State any genuine expiry date or availability limit without inventing urgency.

Then ask when the customer expects to decide and which contact method they prefer. A repair needed tomorrow and a replacement planned for next spring need different follow-up.

For example:

I've sent the estimate for [work]. It includes [scope] and excludes [important exclusion]. When would you like me to check back, and is email the best way to reach you?

If you use text, make sure the customer has agreed to that contact. Identify the business so a callback or message doesn't arrive without context.

Use a short sequence with a purpose for each contact

When the customer hasn't chosen a date, the following is a starting workflow to test, not a research-backed optimum:

  1. After sending: confirm delivery through the agreed channel. An automated delivery receipt doesn't establish that the customer read or understood the quote.
  2. After two business days: offer help with one likely decision, such as scope, timing, or comparing repair and replacement.
  3. After about a week: ask whether to keep the estimate open, schedule a later check-in, or close the follow-up.

Use the customer's agreed timing instead whenever you have it. Stop the sequence when they respond, decline, book, or ask you to stop. Don't stack an automatic text on top of a call someone already handled.

Send something more useful than “just checking in”

Scope question:

Hi [first name], [name] at [company]. Is anything unclear in the [project] estimate? I'm happy to explain what's included before you decide.

Timing question:

You mentioned [timeframe] for the work. Is that still the plan, or would you prefer I check back later?

Close-the-loop message:

Would you like to keep the estimate open, revisit it later, or close the follow-up? Any of those is fine. Let me know what works for you.

Only mention financing, guarantees, or appointment windows when they are real and relevant. Follow-up doesn't give you permission to make a vague estimate sound more certain than it is.

Make estimates easier to compare

Consider a hypothetical furnace replacement. One quote gives a price and equipment name. Another explains the equipment, installation scope, disposal, exclusions, and how scheduling works.

The second quote gives the homeowner more information for a decision. It may still lose on price or timing. The point is to remove avoidable uncertainty, not claim that communication overrides every other factor.

If a customer asks for a lower number, clarify whether they're comparing the same work. Don't cut the price before you understand the difference, and don't assume every lost estimate was a follow-up failure.

Measure estimates separately from new inquiries

Create a list of estimates issued during a defined period. Record the date, service, value, agreed next contact, outcome, and reason when known. Keep open estimates visible rather than treating them as losses immediately.

For that group, calculate accepted estimates ÷ estimates issued × 100 after a suitable decision window. Define how revised or duplicate quotes are counted and use that rule consistently.

Break out urgent and planned work before comparing results. If phone-plus-email follow-up appears to do better than phone alone, check differences in job type and customer preference before crediting the channel.

Research about responding to a new sales inquiry doesn't establish the best schedule for following up on an estimate already issued. Use your own dated records to evaluate this workflow.

Pull your last ten open estimates. Give each one an owner, a clear status, and a useful next action. If the problem starts before a quote is issued, use the separate booking-rate audit. For help reviewing the handoff, see lead response and follow-up.

ai_overviews.ai_quick_answer: Confirm the estimate arrived, ask when and how the customer wants you to follow up, and make each contact useful. Stop when they respond, decline, book, or ask you to stop. Measure issued-estimate outcomes separately from response to new inquiries.
ai_overviews.ai_faqs:
Q: How soon should I follow up on an estimate?
A: Use the timing agreed with the customer. If none is set, test a brief sequence: confirm delivery, offer useful help after two business days, then close the loop after about a week. Adapt it to the job.

Q: Should I stop after one unanswered follow-up?
A: One unanswered contact does not establish the outcome. Use the agreed process and stop when the customer responds, declines, books, or asks you to stop.

Q: How do I measure estimate acceptance?
A: For a defined group, divide accepted estimates by estimates issued and multiply by 100 after an appropriate decision window. Keep pending estimates visible and count revised or duplicate quotes consistently.
ai_overviews.ai_takeaways:
Agree on the next contact when sending the estimate.
Use scope and timing questions instead of repeated empty check-ins.
Track accepted, open, and declined estimates without guessing the reason for silence.

title: Reviews Process: Make Honest Feedback Easy After the Job
searchTitle: Reviews Process: Make Honest Feedback Easy After the Job
excerpt: Build a reviews process with a direct link, optional tap card, neutral request, clear ownership, and delivery checks that work when the shop gets busy.
content:
A useful reviews process has a clear trigger, one owner, and a direct way for customers to leave honest feedback. It should keep working on a busy day without making the front desk pressure someone for a favor.

Keep the practical parts: a visible review link, an optional tap card or QR code, and a well-timed invitation. Let the customer choose whether to review and what to say.

Build the process around the completed job

Choose an objective trigger, such as a completed service visit or collected vehicle. Apply the same invitation rule to customers with positive, mixed, and negative experiences.

Don't send people through a satisfaction score that directs happy customers to Google and everyone else to a private form. A private support channel can be available to everyone alongside the same public review option.

Google's review content policy prohibits incentives, selective positive-review requests, on-site pressure, and requests for specific review content. That rules out asking customers to mention a service keyword or a technician's name for rankings.

Use a tap card as an option, not a demand

A tap card uses NFC to open a link on a compatible phone. A QR code provides another route. Both should open the business's actual review page; test them before putting the sign out.

Simple sign wording:

Want to share your experience? Tap or scan to leave an honest Google review. It's optional, and all feedback is welcome.

Leave the choice with the customer. Don't stand over them, hold up checkout, or require proof that they posted. Offer a normal web link for someone who can't use the card or code.

Google supports review links and QR codes. An NFC card is a way to open that link, not a special Google ranking tool.

Give phone users a clickable link

A QR code in a text can be awkward when the customer is reading on the same phone they'd use to scan it. Use a clickable review link in a message; use the QR code on signage or a printed receipt.

Here's a neutral message for a customer who has agreed to receive this type of text:

Hi [first name], this is [name] at [company]. Thank you for choosing us. If you'd like, you can leave an honest review here: [review link]. All feedback is welcome. Reply STOP to unsubscribe.

Don't treat an invoice phone number as automatic permission for review-request texts. Check the consent and opt-out requirements of the messaging service you use. For example, Twilio's messaging policy requires consent, sender identification, and a working opt-out process; that is provider guidance, not a complete statement of the law.

Choose a reasonable request time after the customer has experienced the work. A next-day request may suit a repair they need to test. That timing is a workflow choice to evaluate, not a universal best-performing hour.

Assign one owner to check that it works

For a hypothetical auto repair shop, the service manager could own the routine: check the completed-job list, confirm contact permissions, send the standard invitation, and review delivery failures. The front desk can point out the optional sign without carrying a review quota.

Once a week, the owner of the process checks:

  • Did the same invitation rule apply to all eligible customers?
  • Did the card, code, and link reach the right profile?
  • Were opt-outs and delivery failures handled?
  • Did public reviews that needed a useful response receive one?

Start with one invitation rather than repeated reminders. Don't chase an individual because you can't find their review; a public display name may not identify the customer, and posting remains their choice.

Measure the process without scoring the customer

Track invitations sent and successfully delivered. Count new public reviews over the same period, but don't assume each came from that period's invitations. Some people review later or arrive through another route.

Use delivered invitations ÷ invitations sent × 100 to check delivery. Treat reviews gained per invitation as an approximate period comparison, not a verified individual conversion rate.

Reviews can help prospective customers understand the business. They don't guarantee a position in Maps, and a service-specific sentence isn't a ranking switch.

Audit your last twenty completed jobs. Look for missed invitations, broken links, and inconsistent selection rules. If the wider profile also needs attention, use the Google Business Profile maintenance checklist.

ai_overviews.ai_quick_answer: Use one objective invitation rule, a direct review link, and an assigned owner. Keep tap cards optional, use a clickable link on phones, and invite honest feedback without steering ratings or wording. Check messaging permission and delivery before automating.
ai_overviews.ai_faqs:
Q: Can I ask only happy customers for a Google review?
A: No. Do not use satisfaction screening to route only positive reviewers to Google. Apply an objective invitation rule without discouraging negative feedback.

Q: Should I ask customers to mention a service or employee?
A: No. Let customers choose their own words. Google prohibits requests for specific review content, including content identifying a staff member.

Q: Should a review-request text contain a QR code?
A: A clickable link is usually easier on the same phone. Use the QR code on a sign or receipt, and send texts only through an appropriate permission and opt-out process.
ai_overviews.ai_takeaways:
Use the same invitation rule regardless of expected sentiment.
A tap card or QR code is optional; a text should provide a clickable link.
Measure invitations and delivery without treating public display names as customer identities.
